title: Descent of a reflexive ideal with principal prime divisors
statement: Let $R\to S$ be a faithfully flat local homomorphism [def-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ring-map] of commutative Noetherian normal local domains [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Local means that the inverse image of the maximal ideal of $S$ is the maximal ideal of $R$. Let $I\subseteq R$ be a nonzero ideal which is reflexive as an $R$-module: evaluation $I\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(\operatorname{Hom}_R(I,R),R)$ is an isomorphism. Let $IS$ be the ideal generated by the image of $I$. Suppose every height-one prime $\mathfrak r$ of $S$ containing $IS$ is principal, where height one means nonzero with no prime strictly between $(0)$ and $\mathfrak r$. Then $IS$ is a principal ideal of $S$, and $I$ is a principal ideal of $R$. The case $I=R$ is included.

source.place: EGA IV4 proof of Theorem 21.14.1, first paragraph, divisorial extension and descent of principality (EGA IV 2.5.2; Bourbaki Algebre commutative VII §1 no.10 Proposition 15 and no.4 Proposition 5). Generic reflexive form: Stacks Tags 0EB9 (more-algebra-lemma-flat-pullback-reflexive), 0AVB (more-algebra-lemma-reflexive-over-normal), and Nakayama 00DV (algebra-lemma-NAK). proof.text: Put $J=IS$. The ideal $I$ is finite by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-submodule-finite], applied to $I\subset R$. Faithful flatness implies flatness. Tensoring $0\to I\to R$ with $S$ gives an injection $I\otimes_RS\to S$ by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-tensor-exact]. It sends $i\otimes s$ to $\varphi(i)s$, so its image is exactly $J$ and it identifies $I\otimes_RS$ with $J$. By [lem-per-flat-base-change-reflexive-modules], $J$ is a finite reflexive $S$-module: both rings are Noetherian domains and $I$ is finite reflexive. Also $J\ne0$: by the exactness-reflection definition of faithful flatness, $I\otimes_RS=0$ would make $0\to I\to0$ exact, hence $I=0$.

Let $H_J$ be the height-one primes of $S$ containing $J$. Choose $0
e b\in J$. By [lem-trf-normal-domain-principal-divisor-kernel], $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is a discrete valuation ring at every height-one prime, and the nonzero valuations of $b$ have finite support. e0$. Thus $H_J$ is finite; enumerate it without repetition as $\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_t$. By the hypothesis choose $x_i\in S$ with $\mathfrak q_i=x_iS$; necessarily $x_i
e0$.

proof.text: For each $i$, the maximal ideal of $S_{\mathfrak q_i}$ is generated by $x_i/1$, so $x_i/1$ is a uniformizer. The ideal $J_{\mathfrak q_i}$ is nonzero, since localization of a domain embeds in its fraction field and $0\ne b\in J$. By the principal-ideal property in [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], write $J_{\mathfrak q_i}=b_iS_{\mathfrak q_i}$ with $b_i\ne0$. By [lem-weil-pbc-dvr-unit-times-uniformizer-power], $b_i=u_i(x_i/1)^{n_i}$ for a unit $u_i$ and an integer $n_i\ge0$. Hence $J_{\mathfrak q_i}=x_i^{n_i}S_{\mathfrak q_i}$.

proof.text: Both $J$ and $cS$ are finite reflexive submodules of $\operatorname{Frac}(S)$. For $J$ this is step 1; for $cS$, multiplication by $c\ne0$ identifies it with $S$. The rank-one free module $S$ is reflexive directly: an $S$-linear map $S\to S$ is multiplication by its value at $1$, and under this identification evaluation on the double dual is the identity. Apply [lem-per-reflexive-height-one-intersection-criterion] to each of $J$ and $cS$. Their localizations agree at every height-one prime by step 4, so their intersections in $\operatorname{Frac}(S)$ agree. Hence $J=cS$, proving the upstairs assertion. If $H_J$ is empty this gives $J=S$ and $c=1$, as required.

Write $\mathfrak m,\mathfrak n$ for the maximal ideals of $R,S$, and $k=R/\mathfrak m$, $l=S/\mathfrak n$. Locality makes the induced unital map $k\to l$ a field homomorphism: its kernel is zero because $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak n)=\mathfrak m$. Put $V=I/\mathfrak mI$. The quotient-tensor identifications [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-over-quotient-ring] and $J=I\otimes_RS$ give $V\otimes_kl\cong J/\mathfrak nJ$. Explicitly this is the composite $V\otimes_kl\cong I\otimes_Rl\cong (I\otimes_RS)\otimes_Sl\cong J/\mathfrak nJ$: its middle map sends $i\otimes\lambda$ to $(i\otimes1)\otimes\lambda$, with inverse $(i\otimes s)\otimes\lambda\mapsto i\otimes\bar s\lambda$. Balancing verifies the two maps are well-defined inverses. Since $J=cS$, its quotient $J/\mathfrak nJ$ is generated over $l$ by the class of $c$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-residue-extension-minimal-generators] with $A=R$, $M=I$, $F=k$, $L=l$, $r=1$. Its finite-generation hypothesis was proved in step 1; the displayed identification gives $\dim_l(V\otimes_kl)\le1$. It follows that $I$ has one $R$-module generator, say $z$, so $I=zR$. This includes $I=R$.

Statement and source: the item is the module form of the first paragraph of the proof of EGA IV4 21.14.1. Read Stacks 0EB9 (more-algebra.tex 5333) and 0AVB (5578); the statement is true. Small cases tested: k[[x,y,z]]/(xy-z^2) with I=(x,z) fails the hypothesis as it should; I=R and a DVR with the identity map work; (x,y) in k[x,y]_(x,y) is not reflexive and not principal, so reflexivity is needed. Steps: step 1 gives J=I⊗S finite, reflexive (0EB9 node) and nonzero (faithful flatness on 0→I→0). Step 2 bounds the height-one primes over J by the finite valuation support of one nonzero b. Step 3 writes each local generator as unit times x_i^{n_i}; a DVR is Noetherian since its ideals are principal. Step 4 is elementary: distinct height-one primes are incomparable, so cS and J agree at every height-one prime. Step 5 applies 0AVB to J and cS; the identification K⊗J=K is routine, and lem-per-divisorial-fractional-module-lattices states the same intersection directly in K. This gives J=cS. Step 6 uses both clauses of the quotient-tensor lemma plus tensor associativity to get V⊗_k l≅J/nJ, of dimension at most 1, so the residue-extension Nakayama node with r=1 gives I=zR. Duplicates: none.
